newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Russia, Ukraine come to agreements.
newsitem.headline: Russia, Ukraine come to agreements.

text.p: Russia and Ukraine ironed out differences between the two states on Wednesday, paving the way for a long-postponed visit by President Boris Yeltsin to Kiev, a spokesman for Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma said.

Spokesman Dmytro Markov told reporters that tense talks between Kuchma and visiting Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, dominated by a row over the disputed Black Sea Fleet and trade issues, ended in a deal.
"After three hours of talks the sides came to decisions which removed all problems standing in the way of the forthcoming visit of the Russian president," Markov said.
Yeltsin is expected to visit Ukraine on Friday and Saturday to sign the friendship treaty between the two Slav pillars of the post-Soviet Commonwealth of Independent States.
"The sides have voiced concern over dramatic decline in the trade turnover and decided to lift all barriers which stand on the way of the bilateral trade," Markov said.

Asked about another painful problem discussed by Chernomyrdin and Kuchma -- the final shareout of the disputed Black Sea Fleet and the fate of its main base of Sevastopol -- Markov said: "Let me repeat, all problems were solved."

Markov said Ukrainian Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko and Chernomyrdin would sign bilateral documents later on Wednesday but did not specify which. Chernomyrdin was expected to leave Kiev late on Wednesday.
Yeltsin has postponed a visit to Kiev to sign a post-Soviet treaty six times since Ukraine became independent from the Soviet Union in 1991.
The key sticking point has been the division and stationing of the Black Sea Fleet, based at the port of Sevastopol on the Crimean peninsula which Moscow transferred to Ukraine from Russia in 1954.

Russia had insisted that Ukraine base its share of the ships 140 km (90 miles) north of Sevastopol, but sources close to the talks in Sevastopol said this week that the two sides had agreed to moor their vessels at different bays at the city.

In Kiev, a foreign ministry official earlier said Chernomyrdin and Lazarenko were expected to sign three documents -- one setting terms for stationing Russian ships in Ukraine, the second dividing the fleet and the third spelling out what Moscow would pay Kiev for rent.
